statements.quote: A training run is a phenomenon you can *watch*, not just a number you report.

The scaling laws are mentioned in the [Hyperparameters](hyperparameters.php) and [Loss](losslab.php) chapters, but a single line — "the loss falls as a power law" — hides most of what actually happens between "initialize the weights" and "the model is done." A run *warms up*, *decays*, *spikes*, and either *settles* or *dies*; the shape of that curve is a direct readout of the choices you made — the model size, the data, the batch, the learning-rate schedule.
This lesson makes that a thing you can touch.
The interactive below is a **training-curve simulator**: set the knobs and watch the loss move toward its theoretical floor, wiggle with the noise of the batch, spike, and recover — or diverge.
Every one of those behaviors is a *lived practice* of the field, and each maps to a named technique you will meet in the sections below.
📘 Simulator: a stylized training run.

statements.quote: All of the above is tuned per model — you pick a learning rate for *this* width, re-tune when you change it, and hope the answer transfers.

\cite[Yang et al. (2022)]{yang2022mup} introduced **μP** (Maximal Update Parametrization), a way of *writing down* the network so that the optimal hyperparameters found on a *tiny* model transfer to a *huge* one essentially unchanged.

The consequence is a new tuning paradigm — tune on a small net where experiments are cheap, then scale the width without re-tuning at all, and the same learning rate, warmup, and schedule keep working.
For teams that train at frontier scale, that transfer is worth a lot: it turns "how do I set the learning rate for a model this size?" into "the answer I already have from the 0.1B model."
| You turn this knob | The curve does this |
| **Batch** ↓ | Cheaper steps, but the curve is noisier ($1/\sqrt{\text{batch}}$ noise).
| **LR schedule** | Shapes the tail: constant flattens, cosine squeezes, WSD holds then drops.
| **Warmup** | Keeps the first, miscalibrated steps from lurching the run.
| **Spikes / high LR** | Recoverable jump vs. divergence — read the shape.
| **μP** | Makes the tuned hyperparameters transfer across model widths.
A training run is not a number; it is a *dynamics*.
The power law tells you where the curve is going, the schedule tells you how it gets there, the batch sets how noisily, and the spike tells you whether it is going to make it.
Watch the curve and you are watching the run.

blocks.quote: \cite[Goyal et al. (2017)]{goyal2017largebatch} made a result that is almost a law: **doubling the batch lets you double the learning rate** and still reach the same loss. The reason is the noise. A minibatch gradient is the true gradient plus noise, and that noise scales as $1/\sqrt{\text{batch}}$ — double the batch and the noise drops by $\sqrt{2}$. A proportionally larger learning rate exactly compensates, so you can trade *more* steps of *smaller* batches for *fewer* steps of *bigger* batches and land at the same place, as long as you hold the product (and the LR) in the right ratio. This is the **linear scaling rule**.
